basis: 14 October 2026, after the team call (Vykintas, Jaideep, Marisha, Gareth), Vykintas's post-call curriculum draft (draft v4), Jaideep's decision deck and Gareth's decisions on it: seventeen lessons and a graduation, one department of the business at a time, in the order a business needs its parts. Every lesson puts something live in the founder's business and installs the AI team that keeps producing it. Built on the AI for Founders quiz (978 answers, 2 to 14 October). Teachers from allocation D, agreed with Vykintas on 29 October and entered in Airtable.
pattern: The problem founders name in that part of the business
The lesson: the finished thing shown first, then the workflow on one example business, while nobody follows along
The lab: the same workflow run on each founder’s own business in three timed builds, with a privacy segment
What changes: something live by Thursday night, and the AI team that keeps producing it

modules.name: Storefront
modules.problem: My business is hard to find, hard to understand and hard to buy from.
modules.installed: A website that beats your three closest competitors, live, with a working lead form; your offer book (ideal customer, competitors, offer ladder, prices); conversion copy with a before and after score; a voice file, which goes into the company brain in week 5; an answer hub that AI search and Google can find, with Search Console tracking it. Four AI teams: web, product marketing, copywriting, SEO and AI search.
modules.changes: A stranger can find the business, on Google and in AI search, understand what it sells and ask to buy, and every page from here on goes live with one sentence.

calls.title: A Website That Beats Your Competitors'
calls.brief: The finished thing first. A site built live in the opening minutes, then the idea every week after runs on: AI is only as good as what you feed it. Your business goes into one folder, and an AI web team builds a site that beats your three closest competitors, with a working lead form. No site yet? The template from onboarding and ten minutes of you talking are enough.
calls.text:
The programme opens with the finished thing: a website built live in the first minutes, before any teaching, from a folder of what the business already has. Then the idea everything after runs on. AI is only as good as what you feed it, and context engineering means feeding it your business once, properly: the old site if there is one, the logo, photos, reviews, ten minutes of you talking about who you serve.

The week's AI team does the rest. The Head of Web runs the workflow in order and asks for what it needs; the designer, the developer and the webmaster build a site that beats your three closest competitors, refined in two or three rounds and previewed on your computer. Because hosting was set up in onboarding, publishing is one sentence; anyone who skipped onboarding goes live in Thursday's lab.

For founders with no website and no brand, the onboarding template and the voice note are the whole input. For founders with a site on WordPress or Squarespace, the new site can replace it or sit on a subdomain. The idea of the week: you have an output and a system. The site is live, and the team that built it is installed for every page you need from here on.

calls.title: Your Site, Live by Thursday
calls.text: A go-live clinic first, for anyone who skipped onboarding: hosting set up together, step by step, from the guide, the Head of Performance pack installed so every later team saves its numbers, and the 30-minute hours log started, so graduation has a before number for everyone. Then three timed builds. The site refined with your own photos and reviews. The site published with one sentence, a custom domain if you want one. The lead form tested end to end with a real enquiry. Before the lab ends the link goes in the community thread and, if you like, on Instagram: a room of live sites is the proof the cohort is real. Privacy segment: what the web team can see, and what never goes on a public page.
calls.win: Your business has a website that beats the competition, live, and you built it

calls.title: Who Buys, What to Sell, What to Charge
calls.brief: A step back after the wow, because every later page, email and ad aims at a buyer and an offer. Your customers researched from your own reviews and call notes, ten competitors researched live, and an offer ladder with prices. Your company's products and services, priced; this is not a personal signature offer.
calls.text:
Every output from here aims at a buyer and an offer. Vague here means generic everywhere. The Head of Product Marketing runs three AI specialists: a customer researcher who reads your reviews, testimonials and call notes for the words buyers actually use; a competitor analyst who researches ten competitors live; and an offer and pricing strategist who builds the offer ladder and the prices.

The output is the offer book: the ideal customer, the competitors, the ladder, the prices. The offers and pricing section goes live on the site the same week, so the lesson ends with something on a page, not a document in a folder.

The line with Expert & Authority: that programme designs the signature offer of a person who is the product. This lesson prices what a company already sells, or is about to sell, and puts it on the site. Founders with no customer data yet start from competitor research and five conversations, and the guide shows how.

calls.title: Your Offer Book, and Prices on the Page
calls.text: Three timed builds. Your reviews, testimonials and call notes fed to the customer researcher. The offer ladder built for your business and the pricing decisions made in the room, with the reasons written down. The offers and pricing section published to your site in one sentence. Privacy segment: customer data, and what to anonymise before it goes into a folder. The lab falls on US Thanksgiving and runs as scheduled; it is recorded, and the week 3 lesson picks up anyone who misses it.
calls.win: Your offers and prices are decided, and live on your site

calls.title: Copy That Turns Visitors Into Buyers
calls.brief: Copy is what sells, and every later page, email and post reuses it. Your site audited, rewritten from the offer book, and audited again, so you can see the score move. Then the voice file: how your company sounds, written once, and the first thing in what becomes your company brain.
calls.text:
The Head of Copywriting runs the workflow: the conversion auditor scores the week 1 site, the conversion copywriter rewrites it from the offer book, the case study writer turns your best customer story into proof, and the auditor scores it again. The before and after number is the lesson's proof.

Then the voice file: how the company sounds, the words it uses and never uses, written from your best pages and your own speech. It is short, it is the company's voice, not a personal brand, and it goes into the company brain in week 5. The answer hub writes in it next week, the inbox team reads it in week 6, the funnel in weeks 8 and 9, the content team in week 10. The lead magnet is promised on the page this week and built in week 8.

The line with Expert & Authority: that programme finds a person's distinctive voice. This lesson writes conversion copy for a company and keeps it consistent.

calls.title: Rewrite, Re-score, Publish
calls.text: Three timed builds. Your own site audited and its score written down. The site rewritten from your offer book and your best customer story, then published in one sentence. The voice file written from your pages and a short voice note, and the site audited again: the before and after score goes in the thread. Privacy segment: testimonials, permissions, and what a customer story can and cannot say.
calls.win: Your site converts better, with the score to prove it

calls.title: Get Recommended by ChatGPT and Google
calls.brief: When people ask an AI who to hire, it answers from pages like the ones you are about to publish. Your buyers' questions mapped from the offer book and your customer research, an answer hub built on your site, and the first articles written and published: free traffic from AI and search into the funnel.
calls.text:
Answer engine optimisation is search for the AI age. The Head of SEO runs a search strategist who maps the questions and objections your buyers actually ask, from the offer book and your customer research; an SEO writer who answers them in articles written in your company's voice; and a search analyst who checks, on a schedule, whether you are found.

The answer hub goes live on your site in one sentence, because publishing was set up in week 1. Results take months and AI citations are hard to measure, so the lesson is honest about both and sets up Google Search Console so there is a number to watch. That is why it comes in week 4: by graduation there are four months of results.

calls.title: Your Answer Hub, Live
calls.text: Three timed builds. Your buyers' questions mapped from the offer book and customer research. The answer hub built and the first article published. Google Search Console connected from the guide. Homework: review the next three to five articles before they go live. Privacy segment: what to publish about clients, and what stays private.
calls.win: Your business is findable by AI search and Google

modules.name: Company brain
modules.problem: Everything I build lives in a different folder, and I keep explaining my business again.
modules.installed: Four weeks of work in one company brain; Claude Code opens there; an AI chief of staff, information officer and operating officer that answer from it; every AI team from here on reads from it and saves back to it.
modules.changes: The business has one memory that every AI team reads from and saves to, and the founder stops re-explaining it.

calls.title: Build a Company Brain That Knows Your Business
calls.brief: Three weeks in, the pain is real: the site in one folder, the offer book in another, the copy and voice file in a third, and every new AI team needs them all. The company brain puts everything in one place, an AI chief of staff answers from it, and every lesson from here builds on it, starting with your inbox next week.
calls.text:
By week 5 the founder has felt the problem the brain solves: four folders, re-attached for every task. It comes early on purpose, late enough for the need to be obvious and early enough that every later lesson builds on it. The lesson shows the pain first, then the template, then the migration, then the C-suite answering questions from it. The chief of staff holds priorities, goals, decisions and briefs; the chief information officer keeps where everything lives clean; the chief operating officer holds processes, projects and the current state.

Every AI team from here reads from the brain and saves back to it: next week the inbox assistant prioritises and drafts replies from the offer book, the copy and the voice file it holds, and the funnel, content, sales and finance teams are all built on it. Website code stays outside the synced brain. A guide covers sharing it with a team, for founders who have one.

calls.title: Move In, and Ask It Anything
calls.text: Privacy segment first: what never goes into the brain, and why. Then three timed builds. Your website, offer book, copy and voice file moved into the brain template. Claude Code opened there and the chief of staff asked five questions about your business, and the gaps it finds written down. The brain's instructions file written so every AI team from next week starts from it.
calls.win: Your company has one brain, and every AI team reads from it

modules.name: Operations: the first system that runs itself
modules.problem: Every message and every decision still comes back to me.
modules.installed: An executive assistant that sorts the inbox and drafts replies every morning, on a schedule, and improves from your feedback; a ranked list of what to automate first. The first AI team that works while you sleep, and the first built on the company brain.
modules.changes: The inbox is sorted and replies are drafted before the founder starts the day, and the founder knows what to automate next.

calls.title: Wake Up to a Sorted Inbox
calls.brief: Operations is the first thing founders asked us to fix, so the first system that runs on its own arrives in week 6, the first week back after the break, straight after the brain. An AI assistant sorts your inbox each morning, prioritises it and drafts replies in your company's voice from what the brain knows, and it gets better every time you correct it. Then the audit that answers the question we heard most: what should I automate first?
calls.text:
Operations is the area founders named first in the quiz, and the inbox is where it lands every morning. This week the first AI team that runs on a schedule arrives: the executive assistant sorts the inbox before you wake and drafts replies; the operations analyst finds the work that eats your week; the continuous improvement manager turns every correction you make into a better instruction for tomorrow.

It comes straight after the brain because the brain is what gives it the context to prioritise and draft: the offer book to answer questions about what you sell and for how much, the copy to answer like your website does, the voice file to sound like your company, and the chief of staff's priorities to know what matters first. Drafts are never sent without you, and it starts with read access only. A schedule that runs on your own computer needs it switched on at that hour; the guide covers what to do when it is not.

The second half is the audit the quiz asked for most: what should I automate first? Your week, ranked by hours and by how safely AI can take it, so the rest of the programme has a list to work from. This lab carries the longest privacy segment of the programme, because this is the week AI first reads something private.

calls.title: Your First Morning Run
calls.text: The longest privacy segment of the programme first, fifteen minutes: what the assistant can read, what it can never do, read-only access, and why nothing is sent without you. Then three timed builds. Email connected and the triage run once by hand. The run scheduled for every morning, with the instruction file it learns from. The automate-first audit run on your own week, and the top three written on your Automation Hub. Three mornings of feedback are the homework.
calls.win: Your inbox is sorted and your replies drafted before you start the day

modules.name: Brand and funnel
modules.problem: People visit and leave, and I never hear from them again.
modules.installed: A brand kit and image library, the site restyled; a funnel chosen for your business model, mapped, with a lead magnet and nurture emails; the funnel live, with a test lead receiving everything.
modules.changes: The business looks like one company everywhere, and a stranger can become a lead and be welcomed without the founder.

calls.title: A Professional Brand Without a Design Agency
calls.brief: Trust is visual before it is verbal. A brand kit made from what you already have, an image library built with the one exception tool, ChatGPT, and the site restyled so it looks like one company. Keep your logo: AI logos are weak, and a clean text logo beats a bad one.
calls.text:
The Creative Director runs a brand designer, an art director and a brand guardian. The brand kit is made from what exists: your logo, your best photos, the colours already on the site. The image library is built in ChatGPT, the one tool outside the stack, because Claude does not make photographs: your own photos turned into editorial shots, product images, backgrounds, the things founders assume cost an agency.

The site is restyled with the kit, and the kit goes into the brain so the funnel, the content and the ads reuse it. The brand guardian checks every later asset against it. The kit goes into the brain beside the voice file from week 3: how the company sounds, and how it looks, in one place.

calls.title: Your Brand Kit, Applied
calls.text: Three timed builds. The brand kit made from your logo, photos and site. An image set made in ChatGPT from your own photos, following the guide. The site restyled with the kit, a browser-tab icon and a link-preview image added, and published in one sentence. Privacy segment: whose photos you can use, and what image tools keep.
calls.win: Your business looks like one company everywhere

calls.title: Design a Funnel That Turns Visitors Into Leads
calls.brief: A site without a path loses its visitors. Your funnel chosen for how you sell: a booked call for services, a purchase for products, a trial for software. Then the lead magnet that earns an email and the nurture emails that do the first conversations for you, written from your offer book, copy and voice file.
calls.text:
Business models need different funnels, so there are three templates: services, where the funnel ends in a booked call; products, where it ends in a purchase; software, where it ends in a trial. The Head of Growth runs a funnel strategist who chooses and maps yours, a lead magnet creator, and an email marketer.

The lead magnet is the one promised on the page in week 3: a checklist, a short guide, a scorecard, made from the offer book. The nurture emails are written from the copy and the voice file and point at the offer. A PDF is the default magnet; a quiz is the stretch, built next week.

The design is done this week and wired next week, so nobody is building and deciding at the same time.

calls.title: Your Magnet and Emails, Written
calls.text: Split by business model: services, products and software in their own rooms from the first minute. Three timed builds. The funnel chosen and mapped for your business. The lead magnet made and checked against the brand kit. The nurture emails written from your offer book and voice file and reviewed. Privacy segment: consent, what you can email and to whom.
calls.win: Your funnel is designed, and the magnet and emails are ready

calls.title: Launch Your Funnel and Collect Leads
calls.brief: A design earns nothing until it is live. The landing page built and published in one sentence, the email platform wired, and a test lead sent all the way through: the page, the magnet, the emails. The quiz version for anyone who wants the stretch.
calls.text:
The Head of Growth now runs the build team: an automation specialist who wires the email platform, a quiz developer for the stretch option, and a funnel tester who sends a test lead through every step. The landing page is built from last week's map and published in one sentence; the form connects to the email platform; the tag starts the nurture sequence.

Kit, free, is what we demonstrate. Every email tool has the same four parts, a form, a tag, a sequence and a broadcast, so founders on another tool follow the adapter guide and change only the last step. The wiring is clicking in a tool, not AI work, so the guide does the explaining and the lab does the unsticking.

calls.title: Funnel Clinic: One Test Lead, End to End
calls.text: Three timed builds. The landing page published. The form wired to the email platform, the tag set, the nurture emails loaded. A test lead sent through: it gets the magnet and the first email, and the screenshot goes in the thread. Anyone stuck on their own email tool is in the adapter room. Privacy segment: the data a form collects, and where it is stored.
calls.win: A stranger can become a lead and be welcomed without you

modules.name: Traffic
modules.problem: Content eats my time, and I do not know which posts or ads bring customers.
modules.installed: A month of posts and carousels from one article, no face needed; a weekly newsletter and content batch with the winners found; a test Meta campaign with a weekly ad report.
modules.changes: People arrive at the funnel from the answer hub, organic content and paid ads, and the founder can see which of them brings customers.

calls.title: One Idea, a Month of Content
calls.brief: Steady visibility without a content team, and without showing your face. One answer article becomes thirty days of posts, carousels and a newsletter, written in your voice from the brain. Production only: growing a following is a different Mastery.
calls.text:
The Head of Content runs a content strategist, a content repurposer and a graphic designer. One article from the answer hub is the source; the repurposer cuts it into posts, carousels and a newsletter in seconds, and the designer turns carousels into images with the brand kit. No face needed, which suits founders who would rather stay behind the business.

This lesson is production, not a social media strategy. Choosing platforms, growing a following and monetising an audience belong to the social media Mastery; here the job is a month of good content, made once, in the company's voice.

calls.title: A Month, Scheduled
calls.text: Three timed builds. One article turned into a month of posts and carousels. The carousels exported as images with the script in the pack. The month reviewed against the voice file and the brand kit, and the first week scheduled in each platform's own scheduler. Privacy segment: what content tools keep, and what to watch when a post names a client.
calls.win: Thirty days of content, no face needed

calls.title: Content That Brings Customers, Week After Week
calls.brief: A list is the one channel you own. The weekly newsletter, next week's content drafted every week, and the post stats read so you know which content brings customers, not just likes.
calls.text:
The Head of Content now runs the weekly rhythm: a newsletter editor who writes from the week's articles and posts, a social media scheduler who drafts next week's batch on a schedule, and a content analyst who reads the post stats and names the winners. Posting itself stays in each platform's own scheduler, because automatic posting breaks easily.

The question this week answers is which content brings customers. The analyst's report feeds the dashboard in week 16.

calls.title: Your Weekly Content Run
calls.text: Three timed builds. The first newsletter written and sent through the email platform. The weekly content batch scheduled to draft itself every week. Post stats exported and read by the analyst, and the winners named. Privacy segment: subscriber data and what the analyst can see.
calls.win: Next week's content drafts itself, and you know what works

calls.title: Run Meta Ads Without an Agency
calls.brief: Organic is free and slow; paid is fast and costs money. Both matter, so this week is paid: an ad spy that studies your competitors' ads, creatives made with your brand kit, a campaign plan, and a small test campaign live with a weekly report. How much to spend stays your decision.
calls.text:
The Media Buyer runs a Meta ad spy that studies what your competitors are running, an ad creative designer who makes creatives from your best content and the brand kit, and a Meta ads analyst who reports every week. The campaign plan aims at the funnel built in weeks 8 and 9.

Meta's account setup is the hardest setup in the programme, so the guide arrives a week early. Not everyone will spend money, and that is fine: the ad spy and the creatives are useful on their own, and the test campaign can run on a very small daily amount.

calls.title: Tracking and Launch Clinic
calls.text: Three timed builds. Your competitors' ads studied by the ad spy. Three creatives made from your best content and checked against the brand kit. Tracking set up from the guide and a test campaign launched on a small daily amount, or saved as a draft if you are not spending yet. Privacy segment: pixels, tracking and what Meta collects.
calls.win: A test campaign live, and a weekly ad report

modules.name: Finance
modules.problem: Invoices, receipts and chasing payment eat hours, and I never see the numbers until it is too late.
modules.installed: An AI accounting agent: invoices and receipts collected into a sheet every week, overdue invoices chased; one more item from the week 6 automate-first list automated with the same pattern.
modules.changes: The books stop being a weekend job, and the money numbers feed the dashboard.

calls.title: Bookkeeping Off Your Desk
calls.brief: Your AI accounting agent. Every week it collects invoices and receipts from your inbox and drive into a sheet and chases overdue invoices, and you send the accountant an export. Then the same pattern applied to one more task from your week 6 automate-first list.
calls.text:
Every business has bills and receipts, even before it has sales, so this automation is the one everyone understands. The Chief Operating Officer runs a bookkeeper and an accounts receivable agent, both on a schedule, and an automation engineer. The bookkeeper reads the inbox and the drive for invoices and receipts, extracts the client, the date and the amount, and fills a sheet; accounts receivable drafts the chase for anything overdue.

The automation engineer then applies the same pattern to one more item from the week 6 list. Finance drew little interest in the quiz, so the lesson is about time back, and the money data it creates feeds the dashboard in week 16. Excel or Google Sheets on your own computer is the default.

calls.title: Invoices In, Overdue Chased
calls.text: Privacy segment first: bank details, what the agent may read, and why it never touches a bank account. Then three timed builds. The invoice collector built and scheduled. The overdue chase drafted and reviewed. One more automation from your list built with the same pattern, and the export for your accountant made.
calls.win: Invoices and receipts filed every week, and overdue ones chased

modules.name: Sales
modules.problem: Leads arrive from everywhere, I chase the wrong ones, and deals die after the first conversation.
modules.installed: A pipeline in the brain, every lead scored, researched and answered the same day, outreach drafted; call prep, call review, proposals and follow-ups written from the brain.
modules.changes: Every lead gets an answer the same day, the founder spends time only on the good ones, and no deal dies for lack of a follow-up.

calls.title: Never Chase a Bad Lead
calls.brief: By now leads arrive from four places: the site, the funnel, content and ads. Your pipeline lives in the brain, every lead is scored and researched, and every one gets a reply the same day, drafted for you. Outreach drafted too, for the leads worth chasing.
calls.text:
Leads come from forms, the inbox and direct messages, and CRMs vary, so the pipeline lives in the brain by default and the skills work with a CRM wherever it lives. The Head of Sales runs a sales development rep who drafts outreach, a lead qualifier who scores every lead on a schedule, and a prospect researcher who prepares the background before you reply.

Marketing has had seven weeks to show results by now, so founders know how much direct selling they need. The reply to every lead is drafted the same day; the founder sends it.

calls.title: Score Your Own Leads
calls.text: Three timed builds. The pipeline set up in the brain, or connected to your own CRM from the guide. Your real leads scored and researched, and the scoring tuned until you agree with it. Same-day replies and outreach drafted for the best five. Privacy segment: personal data about prospects, and what research is fair.
calls.win: Every lead scored, and answered the same day

calls.title: Close More, Chase Less
calls.brief: Deals are lost after the first conversation. Call prep before, a call review after, a proposal written from the brain, and follow-ups that go out until there is an answer.
calls.text:
The Head of Sales runs a sales call coach, a proposal writer and a follow-up manager on a schedule. Before a call, the coach prepares from the pipeline and the brain; after it, the coach reviews the transcript for what worked and what was missed. The proposal writer drafts from the offer book and the call; the follow-up manager drafts every follow-up until there is a yes or a no.

Self-serve products have no calls, so those founders apply the same workflow to partners, wholesale or larger customers.

calls.title: Your Proposal and Follow-Up Kit
calls.text: Three timed builds. One real call transcript reviewed by the coach. A proposal template written from your offer book and used on a live deal. Follow-ups scheduled for every open deal. Privacy segment: recording consent, and transcripts in the brain.
calls.win: Call prep, proposals and follow-ups, written from the brain

modules.name: Cockpit and handover
modules.problem: I cannot see the whole business, and I cannot step back because nobody owns anything but me.
modules.installed: A dashboard of the numbers every department has been saving since onboarding; a Monday briefing with three actions; an owner page for every department; a test week the founder only decides; a graduation where the hours are counted.
modules.changes: The founder runs the company from one screen and one Monday briefing, every system has an owner, and the hours the business needs from the founder are measured against week 0.

calls.title: Run Your Company From One Screen
calls.brief: Every team you built has been saving its numbers since onboarding. This week they become one dashboard, and every Monday a briefing arrives with three things to do. Steering by numbers is what the business running beyond you looks like.
calls.text:
The Head of Performance team arrived in onboarding and has added tracking to every building block since, saving the numbers in the brain. This week the data engineer assembles them on a schedule, the dashboard designer builds one screen, and the CEO briefing arrives every Monday with three actions: do this, try this, spend time here.

Some numbers only come as exports; the guide shows the ten minutes a week they take. The briefing is the page the founder reads in week 17, when deciding is the only job.

calls.title: Your Dashboard and Monday Brief
calls.text: Three timed builds. The saved numbers assembled into your dashboard and the gaps listed. The dashboard built on one screen and published privately. The Monday briefing scheduled, and its first three actions read out in the thread. Privacy segment: who can see the dashboard, and where it lives.
calls.win: One screen, and a Monday briefing with three actions

calls.title: Owners, Then the Week You Only Decide
calls.brief: The promise is a business running beyond you, so this week tests it. Every department gets an owner page: what runs, when, who checks it, what to do when it breaks. Then five working days in which the founder only decides, reading the Monday briefing and the owner pages, and doing none of the work.
calls.text:
Each department built since week 1 gets an owner page: what runs and when, who owns it, a person or an AI team with a human checkpoint, what good looks like, and what to do when it breaks. Founders with a team hand pages to people; solo founders own them and let the AI teams do the work.

Then the test: the five working days from this lesson to graduation, in which the founder only decides. The Monday briefing and the owner pages are the job; the work is not. It is worded carefully. The systems and their owners do the work and the founder reviews and decides; nobody is promised a business with no human in it.

calls.title: Owner Pages, and the Test Week Begins
calls.text: Three timed builds. An owner page written for every department you built. Every scheduled run checked against its owner page and fixed where it fails. The test week planned: the decisions you will make, and the work you will not touch, until graduation. Privacy segment: handing access to people, and taking it back.
calls.win: Every system has an owner, and the week runs on your decisions

calls.title: Graduation and Demo Day
calls.brief: The hours your business needs from you, counted again against the log you kept in onboarding. Then Demo Day: one running system per department shown live, and the next twelve months planned with the AI team you now have.
calls.text: The hours log from onboarding is counted again: the hours the business needs from the founder now against week 0. Then Demo Day, the showcase of what is running: one system per department shown live by the founders who built them, chosen by the cohort. The close looks forward: the next twelve months with the AI team you now have, and what to build next. The word certification is retired; what graduates is a business with systems running in it.

placed.name: Vishen Lakhiani
placed.where: Opens week 1; lessons in weeks 2, 7, 8 and 16; the fast action bonus call; co-hosts graduation
placed.why: Strategy and vision, the decisions a founder makes: what to sell, how the brand looks, which funnel, how to steer. His AI Mastery ratings average 8.59 (287), best on live builds at 9.28 to 9.49, lowest on content creation at 7.87, so he stays off the step-by-step. None of his lessons falls on a Tuesday when he also teaches Expert & Authority; week 1 is twenty minutes.

placed.name: Vykintas Glodenis
placed.where: Every lab and both pre-recorded Get AI-Ready sessions; lessons in weeks 1, 3, 5, 6, 9 and 17; co-hosts the fast action bonus call and graduation
placed.why: Leads the curriculum and takes the builds the rest depends on: the website, the brain, the funnel wiring and the content systems. 472 AI Mastery ratings averaging 9.37, the highest volume of any teacher; his best sessions are integration and system builds.

placed.name: Noelle Russell
placed.why: Getting recommended by ChatGPT and Google in week 4, so the room meets a fourth teacher in the first month; her AI Mastery lessons are on how AI thinks (Talk & Think AI First, 8.85). Closing in week 15: her 9.97 Entrepreneurship Mastery lesson covers speed to lead and follow-up.

placed.name: Ajit Nawalkha
placed.why: Both content lessons, so one teacher carries the content arc: his Entrepreneurship Mastery content lessons scored 9.68 (social content) and 9.39 (newsletters), and he runs this workflow himself. Kept off sales so his January Expert & Authority high-ticket lesson is not repeated.

placed.name: Marisha Lakhiani

electives.title: Build the Software Your Business Needs
electives.text: Idea, spec, build, test, live: the first version of an internal tool or a customer-facing product, built from a spec in the brain, with no logins in version one. Out of the core seventeen because it overlaps AI Mastery's building track; offered as an elective for founders who want it.
electives.format: To be decided: recorded, or an extra live call

onboarding.title: Week 0: Get AI-Ready, pre-recorded and under two hours
onboarding.text: Two pre-recorded sessions with Vykintas, updated as the tools change, so no lesson stops for basics. The first, ready from 5 November: Claude Code set up on a folder, the first AI skills installed, talking instead of typing, the basics of how AI works, hosting ready so publishing is one sentence, and the 30-minute hours log, the number graduation is measured against. The second, ready from 12 November: the go-live walkthrough for hosting, for late buyers and anyone stuck. Before both, on Wednesday 4 November at 7am Pacific (3pm London), the fast action bonus call for early buyers: What to Automate First, Built With Vishen, live with Vishen and Vykintas. Anyone who still cannot publish goes live in the week 1 lab.

lab_format.title: Every week runs the same way
steps: Before the lesson: the week's AI team arrives as one skill pack; installing takes five minutes
Tuesday, the lesson, 90 minutes: the finished thing first, then the whole workflow on one example business. Nobody follows along
Between: the guide and the homework, 30 to 90 minutes, with reminders after the lesson, mid-week and the day before the lab

Thursday, the lab, 90 minutes: three timed builds on each founder's own business with a checkpoint after each, a privacy segment of five to fifteen minutes on what this week's system can see and do, and unsticking in rooms
After the lab: something live, the AI team installed and listed on the Automation Hub with its owner, and its numbers saved for the dashboard

tools: WordPress or Squarespace: move the site, or keep it and publish new pages on a subdomain
Every tool has a form, a tag, a sequence and a broadcast; an adapter guide covers the common ones
A file in the brain, or a spreadsheet
Keep your CRM; the skills work with the pipeline wherever it lives
changelog: Teacher allocation D, agreed with Vykintas on 29 October and entered in the AIF Airtable base: three teachers in the first four weeks (Vishen, Vykintas, Noelle Russell), so the room meets the faculty early. The 2025 AI Mastery cohort met seven teachers in its first eight lessons and kept 62% of its live audience by lesson 8; the 2026 cohort met four and kept 52%.

Getting recommended by ChatGPT and Google moves from week 9 to week 4, into the storefront module, taught by Noelle Russell. Search results take months, so starting in week 4 gives four months of them by graduation. Its questions now come from the offer book and customer research, because the brain and inbox are not built yet.

The company brain moves to week 5 and the sorted inbox to week 6, the first week back after the holiday break. Brand and funnel run weeks 7 to 9; content weeks 10 and 11; Meta ads week 12. Finance, sales and the cockpit keep their weeks.

Noelle Russell teaches findability in week 4 and closing in week 15. Ajit teaches both content lessons, weeks 10 and 11. Vykintas teaches copy in week 3, the inbox in week 6 and the owner pages in week 17. Vishen opens week 1 and teaches weeks 2, 7, 8 and 16. Marisha (12), Sara and Tyler (13) and Joe Stolte (14) are unchanged.

After team feedback (Marta, Marijana) and agreed with Vykintas: copy (week 3) moves from Noelle to Vykintas, since nothing in her record points to conversion copywriting; the inbox (week 6) stays with Vykintas, because it runs on the brain he teaches and stays in Claude Code; Noelle takes findability (week 4) and keeps closing (week 15); Ajit takes both content lessons (weeks 10 and 11), his proven topic. Same number of lessons for everyone. Open: Vishen may take copy in week 3; it would put him in two programmes that morning (Expert & Authority at 9am Pacific), so Vykintas holds it until he answers.

A fast action bonus call for early buyers on Wednesday 4 November, 7am Pacific (3pm London): What to Automate First, Built With Vishen, live with Vishen and Vykintas, the bridge from the summit to kickoff. The recording follows in BlinkLearn.
Both Get AI-Ready sessions are pre-recorded rather than live drop-ins: setup, first skills and the hours log from 5 November; the go-live walkthrough from 12 November.
Customer-facing descriptions for every session are in Airtable, written to the mastery-lesson-descriptions house style; the internal briefs stay here.
